items.title: I can describe magnetism using a field model
items.what: A magnetic field is a region around a magnet where a magnetic force can be experienced. The field model describes this invisible influence using field lines that show direction and relative strength.
items.why: Using a field model allows us to describe and predict magnetic effects without needing to see the actual forces directly. This same model applies to gravity and electric fields, making it a unifying idea in physics.
items.example: Iron filings sprinkled near a bar magnet align themselves along the field lines, making the invisible magnetic field visible as curved lines running from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet.

subtopic.name: Magnetic Field Model
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the field model as a way of describing magnetism. It covers how magnetic fields are represented using field lines, the properties of those field lines, the concepts of dipoles and monopoles, and the difference between uniform and non-uniform fields.
subtopic.why: Understanding the field model is the foundation for analysing all magnetic phenomena in this topic. It allows you to predict directions of forces, interpret diagrams, and connect magnetism with electricity and gravity using a consistent framework.

items.title: I can apply Faraday's three rules for magnetic field lines
items.what: Faraday's rules state that: field lines are continuous loops leaving the north pole and entering the south pole; field lines never cross or intersect each other; and the closeness of field lines indicates the strength of the field.
items.why: These rules make magnetic field diagrams consistent and meaningful. Without them, diagrams could be drawn in contradictory ways that don't reflect real physical behaviour.
items.example: Near the poles of a bar magnet where field lines are drawn close together, the field is strong (about 0.5 T for a school magnet). At a point further away where field lines are spread apart, the field is much weaker.

subtopic.name: Magnetic Field Model
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the field model as a way of describing magnetism. It covers how magnetic fields are represented using field lines, the properties of those field lines, the concepts of dipoles and monopoles, and the difference between uniform and non-uniform fields.
subtopic.why: Understanding the field model is the foundation for analysing all magnetic phenomena in this topic. It allows you to predict directions of forces, interpret diagrams, and connect magnetism with electricity and gravity using a consistent framework.

items.title: I can explain why magnetic fields are dipole fields and compare this to electric and gravitational fields
items.what: A magnetic dipole has two poles (north and south) that always appear together. No isolated magnetic pole (monopole) has ever been observed. Gravity has only monopoles (mass), while electricity has both monopoles (isolated charges) and dipoles (paired charges).
items.why: Understanding the difference between monopoles and dipoles explains why you can never separate the north and south poles of a magnet, and why breaking a magnet always produces two smaller complete magnets.
items.example: If you break a bar magnet in half, each piece becomes a weaker magnet with its own north and south pole. You cannot isolate a single north pole, unlike an electric charge which can exist alone.

subtopic.why: Understanding the field model is the foundation for analysing all magnetic phenomena in this topic. It allows you to predict directions of forces, interpret diagrams, and connect magnetism with electricity and gravity using a consistent framework.

items.title: I can identify and describe magnetic fields as uniform or non-uniform, and as static or changing
items.what: A uniform magnetic field has the same strength and direction at every point; it is shown by parallel, evenly spaced field lines. A non-uniform field varies in strength or direction across space. A static field does not change over time.
items.why: Many calculations in this topic assume a uniform magnetic field. Recognising when a field is uniform (such as between the poles of a U-shaped magnet) allows you to apply formulas confidently.
items.example: The region directly between the poles of a U-shaped magnet produces a nearly uniform static field, represented by parallel equally spaced horizontal lines. The field around a single bar magnet is non-uniform because field lines curve and become less dense further from the poles.

items.title: I can use the arrow convention to represent magnetic fields going into or out of the page
items.what: When a magnetic field is directed into the page, it is represented by a cross (✕), like the tail of an arrow moving away. When it is directed out of the page, it is represented by a dot (•), like the tip of an arrow coming towards you.
items.why: Physics problems often involve three-dimensional field directions that must be shown on a flat page. This convention provides a clear, universal way to communicate field direction in diagrams.
items.example: In a diagram showing an electron moving to the right through a magnetic field directed into the page, you would draw a row of crosses (✕) filling the region to represent the field pointing away from you.

items.title: I can describe the attractive and repulsive interactions between magnetic poles, and compare these to electric and gravitational interactions
items.what: Unlike magnetic poles attract (north attracts south) and like poles repel (north repels north). Electric charges also attract and repel in the same pattern. Gravitational masses, however, only ever attract each other — there is no gravitational repulsion.
items.why: Comparing these three field types reveals that gravity is unique in having only one type of source (mass), while magnetism and electricity involve two types. This comparison is a key part of the study design.
items.example: Two bar magnets with north poles facing each other will push apart. Two bar magnets with a north pole facing a south pole will pull together. Two masses will always pull together, regardless of what they are made of.

subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the field model as a way of describing magnetism. It covers how magnetic fields are represented using field lines, the properties of those field lines, the concepts of dipoles and monopoles, and the difference between uniform and non-uniform fields.
subtopic.why: Understanding the field model is the foundation for analysing all magnetic phenomena in this topic. It allows you to predict directions of forces, interpret diagrams, and connect magnetism with electricity and gravity using a consistent framework.

items.title: I can explain that a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it
items.what: When an electric current flows through a wire, it creates a circular magnetic field around the wire. The field strength is proportional to the current and decreases with distance from the wire.
items.why: This is the discovery Ørsted made in 1820, connecting electricity and magnetism for the first time. It is the principle behind every electromagnet and electric motor.
items.example: A compass placed beside a wire carrying current will deflect so its needle is perpendicular to the wire. When the current is switched off, the compass returns to pointing north because the wire's magnetic field disappears.

subtopic.name: Electromagnetism
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the connection between electric currents and magnetic fields. It includes the magnetic fields produced by straight wires, loops, and solenoids, the use of the right-hand grip rule, and the properties of electromagnets.
subtopic.why: Ørsted's discovery that current produces a magnetic field was one of the most important in physics. It forms the basis of electromagnets, motors, and all electrical machines used in modern technology.

items.title: I can use the right-hand grip rule to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire
items.what: Point the thumb of your right hand in the direction of conventional current flow. Your curled fingers show the direction of the circular magnetic field lines wrapping around the wire.
items.why: This rule gives a reliable method to find field direction in any problem without memorising separate cases. It applies consistently whether the current is horizontal, vertical, or at any angle.
items.example: For a wire carrying current upward (out of the page shown as a dot), grip the wire with the right thumb pointing out. The fingers curl anticlockwise when viewed from the front, so the field runs anticlockwise around the wire.

subtopic.name: Electromagnetism
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the connection between electric currents and magnetic fields. It includes the magnetic fields produced by straight wires, loops, and solenoids, the use of the right-hand grip rule, and the properties of electromagnets.
subtopic.why: Ørsted's discovery that current produces a magnetic field was one of the most important in physics. It forms the basis of electromagnets, motors, and all electrical machines used in modern technology.

items.title: I can predict whether two parallel current-carrying wires will attract or repel each other
items.what: Two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other. Two parallel wires carrying current in opposite directions repel each other. This is because the combined magnetic fields either reinforce or oppose between the wires.
items.why: This interaction is the principle behind the original definition of the ampere, and it demonstrates that magnetic forces act between current-carrying conductors just as they act between permanent magnets.
items.example: Two overhead power lines running parallel and carrying current in the same direction (east to west) will experience a small attractive force toward each other. Engineers must account for this when spacing cables.

subtopic.name: Electromagnetism
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the connection between electric currents and magnetic fields. It includes the magnetic fields produced by straight wires, loops, and solenoids, the use of the right-hand grip rule, and the properties of electromagnets.
subtopic.why: Ørsted's discovery that current produces a magnetic field was one of the most important in physics. It forms the basis of electromagnets, motors, and all electrical machines used in modern technology.

items.title: I can describe the shape and direction of the magnetic field produced by a solenoid
items.what: A solenoid is a coil of wire with many loops. When current flows through it, the individual loop fields combine to produce a strong, nearly uniform field inside the coil and a dipole field outside that resembles a bar magnet.
items.why: Solenoids are the basis of electromagnets and the magnetic components of motors, speakers, and MRI machines. Recognising the solenoid field shape allows you to apply the right-hand grip rule to find its poles.
items.example: A solenoid with 200 turns carrying 2 A produces a much stronger field inside than a single loop carrying the same current. The end where the current flows anticlockwise (when viewed from outside) acts as the north pole.

subtopic.name: Electromagnetism
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the connection between electric currents and magnetic fields. It includes the magnetic fields produced by straight wires, loops, and solenoids, the use of the right-hand grip rule, and the properties of electromagnets.
subtopic.why: Ørsted's discovery that current produces a magnetic field was one of the most important in physics. It forms the basis of electromagnets, motors, and all electrical machines used in modern technology.

items.title: I can describe how an electromagnet is constructed and explain its advantages over a permanent magnet
items.what: An electromagnet is made by placing an iron or steel core inside a solenoid. The iron core concentrates the field, making it up to 1000 times stronger than the solenoid alone. The magnetic effect can be switched on and off and its strength varied by changing the current.
items.why: Electromagnets are far more versatile than permanent magnets for industrial use. They can be turned off to release heavy loads, made stronger for heavy lifting, and shaped into large configurations for specific purposes.
items.example: A scrap metal yard uses a large electromagnet to lift hundreds of kilograms of steel. When the current is switched off, the steel drops into the correct container. A permanent magnet of equivalent strength could not be turned off to release the load.

subtopic.name: Electromagnetism
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the connection between electric currents and magnetic fields. It includes the magnetic fields produced by straight wires, loops, and solenoids, the use of the right-hand grip rule, and the properties of electromagnets.
subtopic.why: Ørsted's discovery that current produces a magnetic field was one of the most important in physics. It forms the basis of electromagnets, motors, and all electrical machines used in modern technology.

items.title: I can explain why a current-carrying wire in an external magnetic field experiences a force
items.what: A current-carrying wire has its own magnetic field. When placed in an external magnetic field, these two fields interact to produce a net force on the wire. By Newton's third law, the wire exerts an equal and opposite force on the magnet.
items.why: This effect is the reverse of Ørsted's discovery: just as current produces a field, a field acts on a current. Understanding both directions of this relationship is necessary for analysing motors and generators.
items.example: A wire carrying current horizontally between the poles of a horseshoe magnet will be pushed upward or downward depending on the current direction. Reversing the current reverses the force direction.

subtopic.name: Forces on Current-Carrying Conductors
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by a current-carrying wire placed in an external magnetic field. It includes using the right-hand slap rule to find force direction and applying the formula F = nIlB to calculate force magnitude.
subtopic.why: The force on a current-carrying conductor is the mechanism by which electrical energy is converted to mechanical energy in motors, speakers, and many other devices. Mastering this section is essential for analysing DC motors.

items.title: I can use the right-hand slap rule to determine the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field
items.what: Hold your right hand flat. Point your thumb in the direction of conventional current and your outstretched fingers in the direction of the magnetic field. Your palm pushes in the direction of the force on the wire.
items.why: The force direction depends on both the current direction and the field direction in a three-dimensional way that is hard to reason through without a systematic rule. The right-hand slap rule gives a reliable, repeatable method.
items.example: For a wire carrying current to the right in a field directed into the page: thumb points right, fingers point into the page, palm faces upward — so the force on the wire is directed upward (toward the top of the page).

subtopic.name: Forces on Current-Carrying Conductors
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by a current-carrying wire placed in an external magnetic field. It includes using the right-hand slap rule to find force direction and applying the formula F = nIlB to calculate force magnitude.
subtopic.why: The force on a current-carrying conductor is the mechanism by which electrical energy is converted to mechanical energy in motors, speakers, and many other devices. Mastering this section is essential for analysing DC motors.

items.title: I can calculate the force on a current-carrying conductor using F = nIlB
items.what: The magnetic force on a conductor is given by F = nIlB, where n is the number of wires, I is the current in amperes, l is the length of wire in metres, and B is the magnetic field strength in tesla. This applies when the current is perpendicular to the field.
items.why: This formula quantifies how increasing current, field strength, wire length, or number of wires each proportionally increases the force. It is used to design motors, calculate torques, and solve exam problems.
items.example: A single wire (n = 1) of length 0.40 m carrying a current of 0.50 A in a field of 0.20 T perpendicular to the wire experiences a force of F = 1 × 0.50 × 0.40 × 0.20 = 0.040 N.

subtopic.name: Forces on Current-Carrying Conductors
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by a current-carrying wire placed in an external magnetic field. It includes using the right-hand slap rule to find force direction and applying the formula F = nIlB to calculate force magnitude.
subtopic.why: The force on a current-carrying conductor is the mechanism by which electrical energy is converted to mechanical energy in motors, speakers, and many other devices. Mastering this section is essential for analysing DC motors.

items.title: I can explain why no magnetic force acts on a wire when it is parallel to the magnetic field
items.what: When the current direction is parallel (or anti-parallel) to the magnetic field, no force is produced. A magnetic force only results when the current and field are perpendicular to each other.
items.why: This is a common source of errors in calculations. Recognising when the angle between current and field is zero (parallel) tells you immediately that the force is zero, with no calculation needed.
items.example: A wire carrying current toward the north in a magnetic field also directed toward the north experiences zero force. Rotating the wire to run east-west (perpendicular to the northward field) would produce the maximum force.

subtopic.name: Forces on Current-Carrying Conductors
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by a current-carrying wire placed in an external magnetic field. It includes using the right-hand slap rule to find force direction and applying the formula F = nIlB to calculate force magnitude.
subtopic.why: The force on a current-carrying conductor is the mechanism by which electrical energy is converted to mechanical energy in motors, speakers, and many other devices. Mastering this section is essential for analysing DC motors.

items.title: I can explain how a current-carrying loop in a magnetic field produces a turning effect
items.what: When a rectangular loop of wire carrying current is placed in a magnetic field, opposite sides of the loop experience forces in opposite directions. These two parallel forces act at a distance from the axis of rotation, creating a turning effect (torque) that causes the loop to rotate.
items.why: This is the fundamental mechanism of a DC motor. The conversion of electrical energy to rotational kinetic energy depends on two equal and opposite forces acting on either side of the loop.
items.example: In a rectangular loop with sides AB and CD parallel to the axis, the right-hand slap rule shows AB is pushed forward and CD is pushed backward. These opposing forces rotate the loop about its axis, just as two hands turning a steering wheel from opposite sides.

subtopic.name: DC Motors and Torque
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the operation of a simple DC motor, including the role of the split ring commutator, the concept of torque, and the qualitative relationship between motor design variables and the torque produced.
subtopic.why: DC motors convert electrical energy into rotational mechanical energy and are found in appliances, vehicles, and industrial machines. Understanding their operation requires linking the force formula, geometry, and the concept of torque.

items.title: I can explain the role of the split ring commutator in a DC motor
items.what: The split ring commutator reverses the direction of current through the coil exactly every half turn. This ensures the forces on the sides of the coil always act in the same rotational direction, allowing the motor to spin continuously rather than reversing back and forth.
items.why: Without the commutator, the coil would rotate 90 degrees to a vertical position and stop (or oscillate). The commutator is what makes a practical, continuously rotating motor possible from a DC power supply.
items.example: As the coil passes through the vertical position (where torque is zero), the commutator switches which half of the split ring connects to each brush. This reversal means the side that was being pushed forward now has its current reversed, so it continues to be pushed forward in the new direction.

subtopic.name: DC Motors and Torque
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the operation of a simple DC motor, including the role of the split ring commutator, the concept of torque, and the qualitative relationship between motor design variables and the torque produced.
subtopic.why: DC motors convert electrical energy into rotational mechanical energy and are found in appliances, vehicles, and industrial machines. Understanding their operation requires linking the force formula, geometry, and the concept of torque.

items.title: I can define torque and calculate it using τ = rF
items.what: Torque (τ) is the turning effect of a force about a pivot point. It equals the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force: τ = rF. Its SI unit is the newton metre (N m).
items.why: Torque determines how effectively a force causes rotation. The same force can produce more or less torque depending on where it is applied. This concept is essential for analysing motor performance and any rotating system.
items.example: A force of 10 N applied 0.30 m from an axis of rotation produces a torque of τ = 0.30 × 10 = 3.0 N m. Applying the same force only 0.10 m from the axis produces only 1.0 N m of torque.

subtopic.name: DC Motors and Torque
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the operation of a simple DC motor, including the role of the split ring commutator, the concept of torque, and the qualitative relationship between motor design variables and the torque produced.
subtopic.why: DC motors convert electrical energy into rotational mechanical energy and are found in appliances, vehicles, and industrial machines. Understanding their operation requires linking the force formula, geometry, and the concept of torque.

items.title: I can explain why torque in a DC motor varies as the coil rotates, including the position of maximum and zero torque
items.what: Torque is maximum when the coil is parallel to the magnetic field because the forces act at the maximum perpendicular distance from the axis. Torque is zero when the coil is perpendicular to the field because the forces act directly through the axis with no lever arm.
items.why: This variation explains why motors rely on angular momentum to carry them through the zero-torque position, and why multi-coil motors (or coils at various angles) are used in practice to produce smoother, more consistent torque.
items.example: At the start of a half-cycle, when the coil plane is parallel to the field, torque is at its maximum. A quarter turn later, when the coil plane is perpendicular to the field, the torque drops to zero and only the spinning momentum keeps the coil moving.

subtopic.name: DC Motors and Torque
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the operation of a simple DC motor, including the role of the split ring commutator, the concept of torque, and the qualitative relationship between motor design variables and the torque produced.
subtopic.why: DC motors convert electrical energy into rotational mechanical energy and are found in appliances, vehicles, and industrial machines. Understanding their operation requires linking the force formula, geometry, and the concept of torque.

items.title: I can describe qualitatively how current, magnetic field strength, and number of loops each affect the torque of a DC motor
items.what: Torque increases if the current through the coil is increased, if the external magnetic field is made stronger, or if the number of loops in the coil is increased. Each of these increases the force on the sides of the coil (F = nIlB), which directly increases the torque.
items.why: Motor designers use these relationships to specify motor performance. A motor needing more turning force can be wound with more loops or operated at higher current, at the cost of more electrical energy input.
items.example: Doubling the number of loops in a motor coil from 10 to 20 doubles the force on each side and therefore doubles the torque. Similarly, doubling the current produces double the force and double the torque.

subtopic.name: DC Motors and Torque
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the operation of a simple DC motor, including the role of the split ring commutator, the concept of torque, and the qualitative relationship between motor design variables and the torque produced.
subtopic.why: DC motors convert electrical energy into rotational mechanical energy and are found in appliances, vehicles, and industrial machines. Understanding their operation requires linking the force formula, geometry, and the concept of torque.

items.title: I can calculate the magnetic force on a moving charged particle using F = qvB
items.what: A charged particle moving through a magnetic field experiences a force given by F = qvB, where q is the charge in coulombs, v is the speed in m/s, and B is the field strength in tesla. This applies when velocity is perpendicular to the field.
items.why: This formula allows calculation of the forces on particles in devices like electron beams and particle accelerators. It also explains why the force is zero when the particle moves parallel to the field.
items.example: An electron (q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s through a field of 0.020 T experiences a force of F = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁶ × 0.020 = 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ N.

subtopic.name: Charged Particles in Magnetic Fields
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by individual moving charged particles in a magnetic field, the circular paths they follow, and the applications of these principles to phenomena such as the aurora and the deflection of particle beams.
subtopic.why: Moving charges in magnetic fields underpin technologies including mass spectrometers, electron microscopes, cathode ray tubes, and medical cyclotrons. They also explain natural phenomena such as Earth's aurora.

items.title: I can determine the direction of the force on a moving charged particle using the right-hand slap rule, accounting for the sign of the charge
items.what: Apply the right-hand slap rule with thumb pointing in the direction of conventional current (the direction a positive charge would move). For a negative charge (such as an electron), the actual force is opposite to the result of the right-hand slap rule.
items.why: The sign of the charge flips the force direction. Students commonly forget to reverse the direction for electrons. Getting this right is essential for predicting circular paths and analysing particle deflections in exams.
items.example: An electron moving to the right through a field into the page: the right-hand slap rule gives an upward force for a positive charge. Since the electron is negative, the actual force on the electron is downward.

subtopic.name: Charged Particles in Magnetic Fields
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by individual moving charged particles in a magnetic field, the circular paths they follow, and the applications of these principles to phenomena such as the aurora and the deflection of particle beams.
subtopic.why: Moving charges in magnetic fields underpin technologies including mass spectrometers, electron microscopes, cathode ray tubes, and medical cyclotrons. They also explain natural phenomena such as Earth's aurora.

items.title: I can explain why a charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field follows a circular path
items.what: The magnetic force always acts perpendicular to the velocity of the particle. This means it changes the direction of motion but never does work on (or speeds up) the particle. The constant-magnitude, direction-changing force produces uniform circular motion.
items.why: Understanding this explains how magnetic fields are used to steer particle beams in accelerators and how mass spectrometers separate ions by mass. It also connects to the circular motion concepts from earlier in the course.
items.example: An electron entering a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the field lines will trace out a complete circle. Its speed stays constant throughout because the force is always at 90° to its velocity, doing no work.

subtopic.name: Charged Particles in Magnetic Fields
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by individual moving charged particles in a magnetic field, the circular paths they follow, and the applications of these principles to phenomena such as the aurora and the deflection of particle beams.
subtopic.why: Moving charges in magnetic fields underpin technologies including mass spectrometers, electron microscopes, cathode ray tubes, and medical cyclotrons. They also explain natural phenomena such as Earth's aurora.

items.title: I can calculate the radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a magnetic field using qvB = mv²/r
items.what: By equating the magnetic force (qvB) to the centripetal force (mv²/r), the radius of circular motion is r = mv/(qB). This shows that a heavier or faster particle curves less, while a stronger field or larger charge produces a tighter curve.
items.why: This formula is used in mass spectrometers to identify particles by their radius, in synchrotrons to control particle paths, and in exam questions combining circular motion with magnetic force.
items.example: An electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s in a field of 0.020 T follows a circular path with radius r = (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.0 × 10⁶) / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.020) = 5.7 × 10⁻⁴ m.

subtopic.name: Charged Particles in Magnetic Fields
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by individual moving charged particles in a magnetic field, the circular paths they follow, and the applications of these principles to phenomena such as the aurora and the deflection of particle beams.
subtopic.why: Moving charges in magnetic fields underpin technologies including mass spectrometers, electron microscopes, cathode ray tubes, and medical cyclotrons. They also explain natural phenomena such as Earth's aurora.

items.title: I can explain how Earth's magnetic field deflects charged particles from the solar wind and causes aurorae
items.what: The solar wind is a stream of charged particles (mainly electrons, protons, and alpha particles) from the Sun. Earth's magnetic field exerts forces on these particles, deflecting most away. Some are directed toward the poles where they collide with atmospheric gases to produce aurorae.
items.why: This application connects the physics of charged particle motion to real-world phenomena and demonstrates why the field model has practical significance beyond the laboratory.
items.example: Charged solar particles moving toward Earth at speeds of hundreds of km/s experience a magnetic force from Earth's field. This curves their paths, with the effect being greatest near the poles where the field lines converge, producing the Aurora Australis and Aurora Borealis.

subtopic.name: Charged Particles in Magnetic Fields
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the force experienced by individual moving charged particles in a magnetic field, the circular paths they follow, and the applications of these principles to phenomena such as the aurora and the deflection of particle beams.
subtopic.why: Moving charges in magnetic fields underpin technologies including mass spectrometers, electron microscopes, cathode ray tubes, and medical cyclotrons. They also explain natural phenomena such as Earth's aurora.

items.title: I can describe how an electron gun accelerates electrons and calculate the speed of electrons using qV = ½mv²
items.what: An electron gun heats a cathode to release electrons, which are then accelerated through a voltage V toward an anode. The work done by the electric field converts to kinetic energy: qV = ½mv², giving v = √(2qV/m).
items.why: The electron gun is the starting point for electron microscopes, cathode ray tubes, and linear accelerators. Understanding it connects electric potential energy to kinetic energy, unifying earlier parts of the course.
items.example: An electron accelerated from rest through 1000 V gains kinetic energy Ek = qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J, and reaches a speed of v = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹) = 1.87 × 10⁷ m/s.

subtopic.name: Particle Accelerators
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how particle accelerators use electric fields to accelerate charged particles and magnetic fields to change their direction. It includes the electron gun, velocity selectors, mass spectrometers, and synchrotrons such as the Australian Synchrotron in Melbourne.
subtopic.why: Particle accelerators are used in medical treatment (linear accelerators for cancer therapy), scientific research (synchrotrons), and diagnostics (mass spectrometers). This section brings together energy, electric field, and magnetic field concepts into a single applied context.

items.title: I can explain that electric fields change the speed of charged particles while magnetic fields change their direction
items.what: An electric field exerts a force along the direction of motion, doing work on the particle and changing its kinetic energy (speed). A magnetic field exerts a force perpendicular to the motion, which changes direction but does no work, so speed stays constant.
items.why: This is the key functional distinction between electric and magnetic fields in accelerators. Linear acceleration is done by electric fields; steering and containing the beam is done by magnetic fields.
items.example: In the Australian Synchrotron, electrons are first accelerated to high speed by electric fields in a linear accelerator, then directed in a circular path by strong magnetic fields. The magnetic fields cannot change the electrons' speed, only their direction.

subtopic.name: Particle Accelerators
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how particle accelerators use electric fields to accelerate charged particles and magnetic fields to change their direction. It includes the electron gun, velocity selectors, mass spectrometers, and synchrotrons such as the Australian Synchrotron in Melbourne.
subtopic.why: Particle accelerators are used in medical treatment (linear accelerators for cancer therapy), scientific research (synchrotrons), and diagnostics (mass spectrometers). This section brings together energy, electric field, and magnetic field concepts into a single applied context.

items.title: I can explain how crossed electric and magnetic fields act as a velocity selector and derive the selected velocity v = E/B
items.what: When a charged particle passes through perpendicular electric and magnetic fields, the electric force (qE) and magnetic force (qvB) act in opposite directions. Only particles where these forces are equal (qE = qvB) travel straight, giving a selected velocity of v = E/B.
items.why: Velocity selectors allow only particles of a specific speed to pass into a detector or analyser. They are used in mass spectrometers and electron microscopes where a precise, known speed is required for accurate results.
items.example: In J.J. Thomson's experiment, he adjusted B until the beam was undeflected. With E = 2.0 × 10⁵ V/m and B = 0.10 T, the selected velocity was v = E/B = 2.0 × 10⁵ / 0.10 = 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s.

subtopic.name: Particle Accelerators
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how particle accelerators use electric fields to accelerate charged particles and magnetic fields to change their direction. It includes the electron gun, velocity selectors, mass spectrometers, and synchrotrons such as the Australian Synchrotron in Melbourne.
subtopic.why: Particle accelerators are used in medical treatment (linear accelerators for cancer therapy), scientific research (synchrotrons), and diagnostics (mass spectrometers). This section brings together energy, electric field, and magnetic field concepts into a single applied context.

items.title: I can explain how a mass spectrometer uses electric and magnetic fields to separate ions by mass
items.what: In a mass spectrometer, ions are accelerated by an electric field to a known speed, then enter a magnetic field. The radius of their circular path depends on mass: r = mv/(qB). Lighter ions curve more tightly, heavier ions less so, separating them for detection.
items.why: Mass spectrometers are used to identify unknown compounds, measure molecular weights, detect trace substances, and even identify new virus strains. This is one of the most direct applications of the charged particle in a magnetic field formula.
items.example: Two isotopes of carbon (carbon-12 and carbon-14) entering the same magnetic field at the same speed will follow arcs of slightly different radii because their masses differ. The separation of where they land on a detector reveals which isotope is which.

items.title: I can describe the role of electric and magnetic fields in a synchrotron and explain why the magnetic field must increase as particles are accelerated
items.what: A synchrotron accelerates particles in a closed circular loop. Electric fields in straight sections increase the particle speed. Magnetic fields in curved sections keep the particles on the circular path. As speed increases, the magnetic field must increase to maintain a constant orbital radius (from r = mv/(qB), if v increases, B must also increase to keep r constant).
items.why: The Australian Synchrotron in Melbourne is a key example of this technology. Understanding synchrotrons shows how the formulas for circular motion, magnetic force, and energy all connect at the frontier of applied physics.
items.example: The Australian Synchrotron accelerates electrons to 99.99999% of the speed of light, increasing the magnetic field progressively to keep them in the 70 m diameter ring. The resulting radiation (from infrared to X-ray) is used for medical and materials research.
